spots.name: Soberanía National Park
spots.label: Soberanía Park

text.directions_text: There is no public transport information to give you a starting point here, so begin from Panama City and get to the park and the Canopy Tower by whatever means suits you. When asking the way, say you want the Canopy Tower, as it is easier to find by name than by the park as a whole. Check the official site before you go for how to reach the tower and whether you need to book. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description: Soberanía National Park is a large stretch of tropical forest beside the Panama Canal, about 25 km from Panama City. It was made a national park in 1980 and covers some 220 square kilometres, with the Chagres River running through it. For a phone photographer the appeal is the mix of green forest and working canal. From the right height you can see treetops rolling away towards the water, with cargo ships passing and the Centennial Bridge small in the distance. The park is also famous for birds, with around 525 species recorded, and Pipeline Road (Camino del Oleoducto), which runs about 17.5 km through the forest, is one of the best-known places to see them. History fans can walk parts of the Camino de Cruces, a 16th-century trail the Spanish used to move gold, where some old stones that once marked the original path still line the way. The classic wide photo is taken from the top deck of the Canopy Tower, so start there for the panorama. Then, if you have time, try the forest roads for close-ups of whatever turns up: toucans, monkeys, coatis or sloths. Wildlife is often far off or half hidden, so be patient and treat any good animal shot as a bonus.
text.access_note: The Canopy Tower deck is on a private lodge, so entry may depend on being a guest or joining a tour; check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Soberanía National Park lies on the banks of the Panama Canal in the provinces of Panamá and Colón, roughly 25 km from Panama City. The Canopy Tower viewpoint is about 1.2 km east of Soberanía National Park, so the park lies to the west of it.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the sky or canal to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the forest does not turn too dark. Try panorama mode for a wide sweep, moving slowly and keeping the phone level. For animals, use the telephoto, tap on the animal to focus and take several shots in a row, since they rarely stay still.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of treetops, sky and canal. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out ships on the canal and the Centennial Bridge in the distance, and for wildlife on the forest roads.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Canopy Tower (top observation deck, about 50 ft above the trees). Treetop canopy stretching out toward the Panama Canal, with cargo ships passing and the Centennial Bridge in the distance. From here the canopy stretches out towards the Panama Canal, with cargo ships passing and the Centennial Bridge in the distance. Soberanía National Park lies to the west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a sensible choice for softer light and more bird and animal activity, but check the official site for visiting times before you plan around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Keep treetops in the foreground to give a sense of height, and leave the ships and bridge as small details in the distance. If you want an alternative to the deck, Semaphore Hill Road is a shaded winding forest road with wildflowers along its edges, good for birds and sloths. Camino del Oleoducto (Pipeline Road) offers monkeys, coatis and birds close to the path.

photo.artist: Katja Schulz from Washington, D. C., USA

spots.name: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute
spots.label: Smithsonian STRI

text.directions_text: From there the institute's waterfront is about 467 m to the south-west. Follow the compass direction and keep to public paths. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
The Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute is a working scientific organisation, and this spot on the map is its waterside base at Puerto de Gamboa, beside the Panama Canal. It is not a big-sights stop. It suits a quiet, atmospheric photo of the harbour edge, with boats, water, low buildings and thick green tropical vegetation behind them.

The photo works best as a wide, calm scene rather than a close-up. Include a bit of foreground, such as a path, railing or water, to give the picture depth. Boats and reflections add interest if the water is still.

Set your phone's gridlines on and keep the horizon level. Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the whole scene, then try a little zoom to pick out the buildings and moored boats without walking closer. Tap the brightest part of the sky or water and lower the exposure slider slightly, so the sky keeps its colour and the greenery doesn't turn too dark. Because this is a research site and a working harbour, stay on public paths, respect any signs, and check the official site before you go to see what access is allowed.
text.access_note: This is a research institute and working harbour area, so access may be restricted or limited; check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Gamboa area of the Panama Canal map, at the Puerto de Gamboa waterfront where the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute has its base.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky is not washed out. If the air is hazy, try Live Photos and choose the best frame afterwards. If the light is dim, hold the phone steady against a solid object and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole waterfront. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the buildings and boats from where you stand. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is only worth using if you walk closer and want to include a lot of foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calzada de Amador (Naos Island section, ocean-facing (south) path, about halfway along Naos). Ships waiting in the anchorage and vessels heading toward the canal locks, seen from a concrete overlook with a railing beside the bike path.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh reflections on the water, and the tropical midday heat is easier to avoid.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower grid line, with the buildings and trees in the middle band. Keep the horizon level. Use a path, railing or the water's edge in the foreground to add depth, and wait for a boat or a bird to pass for a natural focal point.

spots.name: Culebra Cut
spots.label: Culebra Cut

text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 3.4 km north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
The Culebra Cut is the man-made valley that carries the Panama Canal through the Continental Divide. It runs for 12.6 kilometres between the Pedro Miguel lock on the Pacific side and the Chagres River arm of Gatun Lake, with the water 26 metres above sea level. Digging began under the French in 1881, and the Americans later made it far wider, planning a valley up to 540 metres across at the top. Steam shovels broke through on 20 May 1913. The cut was called Gaillard Cut from 1915 to 2000, and the name Culebra came back after the canal was handed over to Panama. It is also known as the Snake Cut.

It photographs well because the scale is easy to see: a straight band of water between steep, cut-away slopes, with the canal's engineering history written into the landscape. A phone does best with simple compositions here. Look for the line of the channel leading away from you, and keep some sky and some hillside in the frame so the depth of the valley shows. If a ship passes, it gives a useful sense of size. Turn on gridlines to keep the water level, and tap on the far bank so the exposure doesn't wash out the sky.
text.access_note: Access and viewing rules for the canal area may change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Inside the Panama Canal, the Culebra Cut is the stretch that crosses the Continental Divide, between the Pedro Miguel lock and the Chagres River arm of Gatun Lake.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far bank to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky looks bright. Try a panorama, moving slowly and keeping the phone level, to catch the length of the cut.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the width of the valley, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the channel. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a ship or the cut slopes on the far side.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 3.4 km north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the slopes than midday sun.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the channel on a lower third line, with the slopes and sky filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the water doesn't tilt. A ship in the middle distance helps show the scale.

spots.alt: Culebra Cut, Panama Canal: the man-made valley. Photo spot
